title: Can all three angles of a triangle be seventy degrees?
description: The three angles of a triangle add to one hundred and eighty degrees. Three angles of seventy degrees add to more than that, so no triangle exists. Two angles of seventy degrees leave forty degrees for the third, and three equal angles are sixty degrees each.
teaching_notes: One idea: the three angles of a triangle always add to one hundred and eighty degrees, so a set of angles that adds to more cannot form a triangle. Watch for students who forget that the three angles must add to exactly one hundred and eighty.

source: Can you construct a triangle all of whose angles are equal to 70°? If two of the angles are 70° what would the third angle be? If all the angles in a triangle have to be equal, then what must its measure be? Explore and find out.
video_script.why: The child knows that the three angles of a triangle make a straight angle and now tests three cases with angles of seventy degrees.
video_script.substitution: Add the angles, compare the sum with one hundred and eighty degrees, and take away or divide to find what is missing.
video_script.anchor: three cases: three angles of seventy degrees, two angles of seventy degrees, and three equal angles
video_script.payoff_line: Two angles of seventy degrees leave forty degrees, and equal angles are sixty degrees each

final_answer.value: No triangle has three angles of 70°; two angles of 70° give a third of 40°; equal angles are 60° each
final_answer.spoken: no triangle has three angles of seventy degrees, two angles of seventy degrees leave forty degrees, and equal angles are sixty degrees each

maths_rules: the three angles of a triangle make a straight angle, so they add to 180°
three angles of 70°: 70° + 70° + 70° = 210°, more than 180°, so no triangle
video_script.design: The three cases stay in the anchor band. The working adds the angles, compares the sum with one hundred and eighty degrees, and finds the missing angle by taking away or dividing.
